questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Counting unblocked backdoor paths in a causal graph
questions.learningObjective: count the open backdoor paths between an exposure and an outcome
questions.stem: A causal graph on five variables has these arrows: Z1 into X, Z1 into Y, Z2 into X, Z2 into Y, X into Y, X into W, and Y into W. A backdoor path is a path that leaves X along an arrow pointing into it. Count the unblocked backdoor paths from X to Y, and give the number as an integer.
questions.explanation: Four simple paths leave X along an arrow pointing into it: X<-Z1->Y, X<-Z2->Y, X<-Z1->W<-Y and X<-Z2->W<-Y. The first two are open, because Z1 and Z2 each sit on the path as a non-collider and nothing in the path is conditioned on. The other two pass through W, which has an arrow into it from X and an arrow into it from Y, so W is a collider on those paths and no descendant of W is conditioned on, which leaves them blocked. That leaves 2 open backdoor paths. The count matters because a path left open is a route by which a cause of X that is not X itself can reach Y, so an estimate that leaves any of these routes open is mixing the effect of X with the effect of whatever produced Z1 and Z2.
questions.hint: A path is closed when it passes through a conditioned variable that is not a collider, or a collider with a conditioned descendant. Check each path against that rule.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Adjusting for a collider
questions.learningObjective: explain what conditioning on a collider does to an estimate
questions.stem: In a graph with arrows X into Y, X into W and Y into W, a researcher builds a regression of the outcome on the exposure, the mediator W and one other covariate. What does including W do?

options.text: It opens a route that ran from the exposure through W to the outcome, so the estimate picks up an association the exposure never caused and moves away from the total effect
It removes the path from the exposure to the outcome, so the estimate becomes a clean measure of the total effect the study is asking about
options.misconception: treats a collider as if it blocked a causal path rather than opening one

options.text: It has no effect at all, because a variable that is downstream of both the exposure and the outcome cannot be related to either of them
options.misconception: believes a common effect of two variables cannot be related to either

options.text: It makes the estimate unbiased whatever else is in the model, because a variable measured on every unit of the sample cannot introduce bias
options.misconception: assumes complete measurement rules out the collider problem

questions.explanation: W is a common effect of the exposure and the outcome, so every path that runs from the exposure through W to the outcome is blocked as long as nothing on it is conditioned on, and conditioning on W opens it. The additional covariate W in the regression is that conditioning, so the estimate moves further from the exposure's own effect and towards the part of it that also moves W, which is not what the study is about. The general rule is that a variable on the causal path from exposure to outcome is a mediator and a common effect of the two is a collider, and neither belongs in a set of covariates chosen to estimate the total effect. In this graph there are four subsets of the three candidate covariates that include W, and every one of them is compromised by the same opening.
questions.hint: Work out which nodes are colliders before deciding which covariates to include.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Change in an estimate after adding a measured confounder
questions.learningObjective: compute how far a crude slope overstates an effect
questions.stem: A simulation builds an outcome in which the true effect of the exposure on the outcome is 0.50 units. One variable confounds the exposure and the outcome and is measured, though recorded with error. Regressing the outcome on the exposure alone gives a slope of 0.8388. Adding the measured confounder to the regression gives a slope of 0.5009. By how much does the crude slope overstate the true effect? Give the answer to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: The crude slope of 0.8388 compares units that differ not only in the exposure but in the confounder as well, and because the confounder also drives the outcome, the difference picks up the confounder as well as the exposure, which is why it exceeds the true effect. Adding the measured confounder brings the slope to 0.5009, within 0.0009 of the structural 0.50 that was built into the data, so the overstatement is 0.8388 minus 0.5009, that is 0.3407. In a linear model a confounder recorded with error conditions on the same information as the confounder itself, which is why the residual overstatement here is negligible. The practical point is that the size of the shift is the diagnostic: a large shift says the comparison was confounded, and a small one is not proof that nothing unmeasured remains, only that what was measured accounted for what moved.
questions.hint: Subtract the adjusted slope from the crude slope. The truth is not needed to do it.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A mediator on the causal path
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a confounder from a mediator by its position in a graph
questions.stem: A study estimates the effect of a training programme on later earnings. A graph of the design includes a variable for hours of study completed during the programme. What does controlling for it do to the estimate?

options.text: It blocks the route through which the programme works, so the number it produces answers a narrower question than the total effect the study was designed to estimate
It removes a route into the outcome that had nothing to do with the programme, so the number it produces is a cleaner measure of the programme's effect
options.misconception: treats a mediator as though it were a confounder

options.text: It has no effect on the estimate, because a variable the programme itself changes cannot be associated with the outcome
options.misconception: believes a variable the treatment changes cannot predict the outcome

options.text: It doubles the effective sample size, because the two routes from programme to earnings now supply two independent estimates of the effect
options.misconception: invents a precision gain from adding a covariate to a model

questions.explanation: Hours of study sit between the programme and later earnings, so they are a mediator rather than a confounder: the programme is what moves them, and they are what moves earnings. Holding them fixed blocks the route through which the programme operates, so the resulting number answers the narrower question of what the programme would have done for a unit with the same study hours whatever the programme was, which is not the question the study was set up to ask. A confounder instead has arrows into both the programme and earnings, so conditioning on it removes a route that had nothing to do with the programme and leaves the programme's own route intact. The two therefore need opposite treatment, and a variable's position in a graph, not how plausible it looks as a control, is what tells them apart.
questions.hint: Ask whether the programme changes the variable, or whether the variable changes whether a unit gets the programme.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Marginal and stratified risk differences in one table
questions.learningObjective: compute a marginal risk difference from a two-by-two-by-two table
questions.stem: An observational cohort of 400 people records treatment and a severity score from an earlier episode, and each cell gives the number who had the outcome out of the number in the cell. Severity 0: treated 48 of 160, untreated 4 of 40. Severity 1: treated 8 of 40, untreated 112 of 160. Compute the marginal risk difference, treated minus untreated, over the whole sample. Give the answer to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: The treated arm holds 200 people with 104 outcomes, so its risk is 104 over 200, that is 0.5200, and the untreated arm holds 200 with 58 outcomes, a risk of 0.2900. The difference is -0.3. Inside the severity strata the differences are 0.2 at severity 0 and -0.5 at severity 1, so the marginal figure has the opposite sign to one of them. The reason is that the marginal difference is a difference of two mixtures rather than a mixture of the differences: the treated arm is 0.20 severe while the untreated arm is 0.80 severe, and severity predicts the outcome strongly. Weighting the two stratum differences by the treated arm alone would give 0.06 and by the untreated arm alone -0.36, neither of which is the marginal. The table checks out: the four denominators sum to 400 and the four outcome counts to 172.
questions.hint: Pool each arm's events and its denominators before subtracting; the strata do not enter this figure.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Reading a marginal effect that reverses inside every stratum
questions.learningObjective: state what a reversal between marginal and stratified estimates establishes
questions.stem: A cohort table shows a marginal risk difference of -0.3 in favour of treatment, and differences of 0.2 and -0.5 in the two strata of an earlier severity score. A draft concludes that the treatment reduces the outcome. What is the right reading?

options.text: The pooled figure depends on how the severity strata happen to be distributed across the arms, so it summarises none of them and the stratified figures are the ones to report
The pooled figure is the one to report, because a marginal estimate is by construction the average of the population the study enrolled and is therefore the most general of the two
options.misconception: treats an unadjusted average as automatically the most general estimate

options.text: The two results contradict each other, so the study has an error in the coding of the severity score and cannot be reported at all
options.misconception: reads a reversal between weightings as a coding error

options.text: The stratified figures are the biased ones, because splitting the sample in two always inflates the variance of an effect and therefore biases it away from the truth
options.misconception: confuses a variance cost from splitting with a bias

questions.explanation: The marginal figure of -0.3 has the opposite sign to the 0.2 difference in the mild stratum, so the pooled number is not a summary of the strata and its direction depends on how the two arms happen to be mixed. That happens when the stratum predicts the outcome strongly and is distributed unevenly across the arms, and the treated arm here is 20% severe against 80% in the untreated arm, which is exactly the situation adjustment is for. Neither the marginal nor either stratum on its own settles the question, and the honest report gives the stratum-specific figures, the imbalance, and the fact that the crude comparison cannot be read as an effect. Reading the pooled figure as a summary of the stratified ones is a mistake about what an unadjusted comparison is, and it is a mistake that a single pooled number invites.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the pooled figure if the arms happened to have the same severity mix.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Adjusting for a consequence of the outcome
questions.learningObjective: explain why adjusting for a downstream consequence of the outcome distorts an estimate
questions.stem: A cohort of surgical patients records the operation, the complication rate, and each patient's length of stay in hospital. Length of stay is later shown to be a consequence of whether a complication occurred. What follows for the analysis?

options.text: It is a consequence of the exposure and a common effect of the exposure and the outcome, so conditioning on it opens a route and the estimate stops being the total effect
It is a consequence of the exposure, so conditioning on it simply removes the part of the effect that runs through it and leaves the direct effect, which is also of interest
options.misconception: offers a direct effect where the study asked for the total effect

options.text: It is a consequence of the exposure, so it is a collider and the model should exclude it, which the graph shows and which the analysis already does
options.misconception: names the right problem and then claims the analysis already avoids it

options.text: It is measured after the exposure, so it cannot be related to the outcome and its inclusion is harmless to the estimate
options.misconception: believes timing after the exposure rules out association with it

questions.explanation: Length of stay is downstream of the exposure and also downstream of a cause of the outcome, which makes it both a consequence of the exposure and a collider between the exposure and the outcome, because complications affect both the complication rate and the length of stay. Conditioning on it therefore opens a route from the exposure to the outcome that did not exist in the data as collected, and the resulting estimate describes an association conditional on a quantity that the exposure itself helps to determine. Variables that lie after the exposure on a causal route carry this problem whatever their substantive plausibility, and the general test is positional: a covariate chosen to estimate a total effect must be a cause of the exposure and of the outcome, and must not be caused by either.
questions.hint: Place the variable on the graph first. Where it sits decides whether it belongs in the covariate set.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Sequence for drawing a causal graph before choosing covariates
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps from a design to an adjustment set
questions.stem: A team has a research question, a dataset with several candidate covariates, and no graph. Put these steps in the order they should be carried out.

options.text: List the exposure, the outcome and the time origin for each, so the graph describes a specific interval rather than a lifetime of exposure
List every variable the dataset holds that could plausibly be a cause of either the exposure or the outcome, treating this as a list of candidates and not of controls
Draw the arrows using what the field knows about the mechanisms, marking which arrows are assumed and which are established
Read off the sets that block every backdoor path, and discard any set containing a mediator, a collider or a consequence of the outcome
Pick one such set, noting that adding a pure cause of the outcome changes precision without changing the target

questions.explanation: The graph comes before the covariate list, because the covariate list is a consequence of what the graph says is a cause of both the exposure and the outcome, and building it first guarantees that the answer is decided before the evidence is seen. Listing what the data contain is worth doing but it produces candidates, not a set. Drawing arrows uses substantive knowledge of the field, not the data, and a variable's status as a cause is a claim about the world that a data pattern cannot settle. Blocking every backdoor path then follows, and only after that is a set written down. Choosing among sets that differ by irrelevant variables is the last step, and it is the one with the least consequence, because adding a cause of the outcome that is not a cause of the exposure changes the variance without changing the target.
questions.hint: Ask which step fixes the target quantity that the whole exercise is estimating.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Counting covariate subsets that leave a backdoor path open
questions.learningObjective: count the covariate subsets that fail to block a backdoor path
questions.stem: A graph has arrows Z1 into X, Z1 into Y, Z2 into X, Z2 into Y, X into Y, and Z3 into Y only. The analysis team can adjust for any subset of the three candidate covariates Z1, Z2 and Z3. Of the eight subsets, how many leave at least one backdoor path from X to Y open? Give the number as an integer.
questions.explanation: Each of Z1 and Z2 is on its own backdoor path, X<-Z1->Y and X<-Z2->Y, and on each of those the confounder sits as a non-collider, so the path is open until that variable is conditioned on. A subset therefore blocks both doors only if it contains Z1 and Z2, and Z3 is irrelevant to the question because nothing points from it to X. Of the eight subsets, the two that contain both Z1 and Z2, namely Z1 with Z2 and Z1 with Z2 with Z3, block the paths, and the other 6 leave at least one open. Note that including Z3 in a valid set does no harm, because conditioning on a cause of the outcome that is not a cause of the exposure costs precision and buys nothing, and a rule that only accepts the smallest set has to be justified rather than assumed.
questions.hint: Count the subsets that are missing Z1 or missing Z2, and note that Z3 changes nothing.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What the front-door criterion buys
questions.learningObjective: state the three requirements of a front-door identification strategy
questions.stem: A causal graph has an unmeasured common cause of X and Y, a variable M through which all of X's effect on Y must pass, and no unmeasured common cause of M and Y once X is held fixed. The team cannot measure the unmeasured variable. What does the graph license?

options.text: The effect of X on Y is identified from X, M and the marginal distribution of X, because the mediator is unconfounded with X, fully mediates, and is unconfounded with Y given X
Nothing is identified, because any unmeasured common cause of X and Y contaminates every estimate no matter how many mediators are measured
options.misconception: denies identification where a mediating structure can supply it

options.text: The effect of X on M is the effect of X on Y, because a mediator that carries all of the effect must pass on its full size to the outcome
options.misconception: reads complete mediation as though the effect were passed on unchanged

options.text: The effect is identified only if M is measured without error, because any error in M leaves the same unmeasured confounding the strategy was meant to remove
options.misconception: insists a deterministic relationship is needed to identify the effect

questions.explanation: Those three features are the front-door criterion, and together they identify the effect of X on Y without the unmeasured variable ever entering the analysis. The identification runs in three steps: the effect of X on M is estimable because nothing unmeasured links them, the effect of M on Y is estimable once X is held fixed because the second requirement says X is the only unblocked route into Y from M, and combining the two in the usual weighted average over the marginal distribution of X recovers the effect of X on Y. Each requirement is doing distinct work, and dropping any one of them leaves the combination unidentified, which is why a single observed mediator is not a general solution to unmeasured confounding. The requirement that the mediator carry all of the effect is the one most often assumed without argument, and if some of the effect bypasses M the weighted average no longer equals the total effect.
questions.hint: Check each of the three features separately, because each is a separate requirement rather than a detail.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Front-door weighted average from four conditional probabilities
questions.learningObjective: compute a front-door contrast from conditional probabilities
questions.stem: In a front-door structure the fitted probabilities are P(M=1 given X=1) = 0.5999, P(M=1 given X=0) = 0.1998, P(Y=1 given M=1) = 0.4997 and P(Y=1 given M=0) = 0.1996, and the marginal share with X=1 is 0.4399. The study reports a difference on the probability scale. Compute the front-door difference in the probability of the outcome between X=1 and X=0. Give the answer to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: The front-door quantity for a fixed value of the exposure averages the mediator's contribution to the outcome over the mediator's distribution at that value of the exposure, so at X=1 it is 0.5999 times 0.4997 plus one minus 0.5999 times 0.1996, and at X=0 it is 0.1998 times 0.4997 plus one minus 0.1998 times 0.1996. Subtracting the second from the first gives 0.1201. The marginal share of 0.4399 is not needed for a difference between two values of the exposure, because it appears identically in both and cancels, and it would be needed for a level rather than a contrast. The figure is the average effect of the mediator's distribution rather than a single mediator value, and a shortcut that multiplied the two coefficients directly would be wrong, since the effect of the mediator on the outcome is not constant across mediator levels.
questions.hint: Build each level as a weighted average of the two outcome probabilities, weighting by the mediator probabilities at that exposure level, then subtract.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Positivity as a property of the data, not of the model
questions.learningObjective: state what a lack of common support means for an estimate
questions.stem: A propensity model assigns some units a probability of treatment of 0.97 and others 0.02. A researcher proposes to identify the effect by weighting every unit to the marginal treatment rate. What does this pair of probabilities rule out?

options.text: It rules out estimating the missing arm for those units from these data, because weighting cannot supply an outcome that was never observed in the other arm
It rules out nothing once weights are applied, because inverse weighting is specifically designed to correct for any imbalance including a near-certain arm assignment
options.misconception: believes weighting manufactures the unobserved counterfactual

options.text: It requires a larger sample from the same sources, since the imbalance is a matter of precision rather than of which arm exists
options.misconception: misreads a structural absence as a shortage of observations

options.text: It calls for replacing the propensity model with one that is better specified, since the imbalance indicates that the current functional form is wrong
options.misconception: assumes structural non-overlap is a symptom of misspecification

questions.explanation: To estimate the counterfactual outcome for a unit one needs the other arm to be possible for units like it, and a probability of 0.97 for some units means the untreated state is close to impossible for them, while 0.02 for others means the treated state is. Weighting cannot create observations that the design never produced: the weights for those units are large but multiply outcomes that were never observed in the other arm, so the estimate for the population as a whole is a projection driven by the model's shape over a region with no data. The two remedies are different in kind. Restricting the estimand to the units where both arms occur, which is a common support, changes the question. Extending the model beyond the data changes the assumptions the estimate rests on, and that is a modelling decision to be stated rather than a computation.
questions.hint: Ask what the analysis would do for a unit with the value that its own propensity says never happens.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Common support and the sample it discards
questions.learningObjective: count the units that fall outside a stated common support
questions.stem: A propensity model is fitted to a cohort of 200 people with a single measured confounder. The fitted propensities run from 0.2295 to 0.9061. The team keeps only units whose propensity lies between 0.20 and 0.80 inclusive. How many units are discarded? Give the number as an integer.
questions.explanation: Of the 200 people, 31 have a fitted propensity below 0.20 or above 0.80, leaving 169. The split is uneven between the arms: 27 of the discarded are people who were actually treated and 4 are people who were not, because the extremes of the propensity distribution are where the arms are least similar and the imbalance runs in that direction. Restricting the analysis to the region where both arms occur is what makes the comparison meaningful there, and the price is that the resulting number answers a question about the 169 units rather than about all 200. Dropping the units is not a way of making the problem smaller, since the discarded units are exactly the ones whose counterfactual outcome cannot be learned from these data, and a report that quietly narrows the population without saying so turns a limitation into a hidden change of target.
questions.hint: Count the units with a propensity outside the interval, then split that count by arm.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Reading a table of nested adjusted estimates
questions.learningObjective: read a sequence of adjusted estimates for what it does and does not show
questions.stem: A cohort study reports a crude slope of 0.84 between the exposure and the outcome, a slope of 0.63 after adding one measured confounder, 0.52 after adding a second, and 0.50 after adding a third. The outcome was generated with a true effect of 0.50. What does the sequence support?

options.text: It supports the view that the measured covariates account for the confounding present, while leaving open whether an unmeasured confounder acts through those same variables
It shows the third confounder was essential, because the estimate only reaches the true value once that variable enters the model
options.misconception: reads a small last step as proof of necessity

options.text: It rules out unmeasured confounding, because any unmeasured confounder would have shifted at least one of the four estimates away from the truth
options.misconception: claims the design can exclude what it was never able to observe

options.text: It shows the model is correctly specified, since a specification error would have left the sequence still moving after the last covariate was added
options.misconception: treats a settled sequence as proof of correct functional form

questions.explanation: The estimates move from 0.84 to 0.50 as confounders are added and settle close to the value the data were built with, so the measured covariates account for the confounding that was present and the residual is small. That is the most a nested sequence can establish. It cannot show that the third confounder was necessary, because a set that omits it and a set that includes it give the same answer here, and a single variable that is a proxy for two mechanisms can absorb both. Nor can it show that no unmeasured confounder remains, because an unmeasured confounder acting through the same variables as a measured one is absorbed by them and leaves the sequence exactly as it stands. A shift of this size is a reason to think the comparison is not badly confounded. It is not a certificate, and the gap between a small residual and a zero residual is not something this design can resolve.
questions.hint: Ask what an unmeasured confounder would have to do in order to leave this sequence untouched.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A graph that makes a published adjustment unjustified
questions.learningObjective: recognise an adjustment that the study's own graph rules out
questions.stem: A published cohort study of a workplace safety programme reports that the programme reduces injuries by 0.42, and states that the model adjusted for age, tenure, shift pattern and prior injury count. A field diagram shows that the safety programme's own rollout determined which employees were assigned to the night shift, and that the night shift affected both injury risk and prior injury reporting. What is the defect?

options.text: Shift pattern is a consequence of the programme and a common cause of injury and of the reported prior injuries, so adjusting for it opens a route and the reported number is not the programme's effect
The defect is that the study adjusted for four covariates, because adjustment sets of that size are too large to be specified reliably from observational data
options.misconception: invents a sample-size objection to the number of covariates

options.text: The defect is that prior injury count is a pre-exposure measure, because adjusting for a pre-exposure measure of the outcome is always forbidden in a cohort study
options.misconception: claims a pre-exposure covariate is always impermissible

options.text: There is no defect, because the field diagram describes how the programme was rolled out and the rollout is part of the exposure rather than a confounder of it
options.misconception: rules out a collider by calling the offending arrow a rollout

questions.explanation: Rollout determined shift pattern, so shift pattern is a consequence of the exposure, and it is also a common cause of the outcome and of the prior-injury count that is adjusted for. Adjusting for it therefore opens a route from the programme to the outcome that was closed in the data as collected, and the adjusted figure no longer estimates the programme's effect. The diagram also shows the route that makes the adjustment look attractive, because shift genuinely predicts injury, so the covariate is substantively plausible and the defect is invisible from the variable list alone. The remaining covariates, age and tenure, are causes of both the exposure and the outcome and would have been reasonable to include. The fix is to leave shift pattern out, report the crude comparison alongside, and say which quantity the published number fails to describe.
questions.hint: Trace each adjusted variable back and ask whether the programme could have changed it.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Why a randomised comparison tolerates an imprecise balance check
questions.learningObjective: explain what randomisation does and does not make adjustable
questions.stem: A randomised trial turns out to have 54 per cent men in the treatment arm and 46 per cent in the control arm. A colleague proposes adding sex to the analysis model as a covariate. What is the right response?

options.text: The imbalance is chance and the estimate stays unbiased either way, so sex is worth including for precision but excluding the imbalanced arm is not, because that conditions on the randomisation itself
The imbalance is chance, so the model must include sex to remove it, and any arm that ends up with a statistically different mean must be excluded as a sign of allocation failure
options.misconception: accepts significance-based exclusion of an arm

options.text: The imbalance means the randomisation failed, so the trial's conclusion is void until a new randomisation is performed and this one is discarded
options.misconception: treats a chance imbalance as evidence the mechanism failed

options.text: Sex is a baseline covariate, so it cannot be adjusted for, because adjusting for a baseline variable in a trial is the same as conditioning on the randomisation
options.misconception: claims baseline adjustment conditions on the randomisation

questions.explanation: Randomisation makes sex independent of assignment in expectation, so the imbalance is chance and carries no information about the treatment, and the estimate stays unbiased whether or not sex is in the model. What randomisation does buy is protection against confounding by every pre-exposure variable at once, including the ones nobody thought to write down, which is why a trial can report a crude comparison. The two imbalance remedies are not equivalent. Adjusting for a baseline covariate is a precision device, and it is the standard recommendation because it can only reduce variance when the model is right. Excluding by significance is different in kind: it conditions on a realisation of the randomisation, and because the excluded arm is then the arm that happened to be imbalanced, the retained comparison carries a bias of its own. Conditioning on a post-randomisation variable is a third thing again, and can do real damage to a valid comparison.
questions.hint: Ask whether the imbalance reflects a real difference or the luck of the draw, and what the remedy does to the estimate.

questions.topic: Inverse probability weighted contrast from a cell table
questions.learningObjective: compute an inverse-probability-weighted average treatment effect
questions.stem: A cohort of 400 people is cross-tabulated by a measured confounder Z and by exposure. Z=0: 20 of 50 exposed have the outcome, 15 of 50 unexposed do. Z=1: 60 of 100 exposed do, 40 of 200 unexposed do. Treatment is assigned independently of Z within each stratum, so the propensity score equals the exposed share of the stratum. Compute the average treatment effect by inverse probability weighting as the average over all 400 people of the exposed outcome divided by the propensity minus the unexposed outcome divided by one minus it. Give the answer to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: The exposed arm holds 150 people with 80 outcomes and the unexposed arm 250 people with 55, so the crude risk difference is 0.5333 minus 0.2200, which is 0.3133. The propensity score is 0.5000 at Z=0, since 50 of that stratum's 100 people are exposed, and 0.3333 at Z=1, since 100 of 300 are. Weighting the exposed outcomes by the reciprocal of those scores and the unexposed by the reciprocal of their complements and taking the difference over all 400 people gives 0.325. A second route gives the same number: the stratum-specific differences are 0.1 and 0.4, and weighting them by stratum size, 100 of 400 and 300 of 400, gives 0.325. The small gap between 0.3133 and 0.325 is the whole of the confounding by Z in this table.
questions.hint: Sum the weighted exposed outcomes and the weighted unexposed outcomes, then divide their difference by the sample size rather than by a treated count.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a causal graph says about unmeasured confounding
questions.learningObjective: state the limit of a graph that contains no unmeasured arrows
questions.stem: A team draws a graph containing only variables they measured, and confirms that every backdoor path is blocked by their covariate set. A reviewer asks what the diagram cannot tell them. What is the right answer?

options.text: It shows the measured set blocks every path the team can see, and a path through a variable they never recorded appears in no diagram, so the unmeasured case needs a design or a sensitivity analysis
It shows the adjustment is valid, because a confounding path must pass through a variable that appears in at least one of the two analysis models
options.misconception: assumes a confounder must be in the model to exist

options.text: It shows the estimate is unbiased under the assumption that the graph is complete, so the only remaining task is to report the assumption clearly
options.misconception: leaves a conditional statement standing in for an established one

options.text: It shows the opposite, that no measured covariate is needed, since a complete diagram implies the exposure is unconfounded by construction
options.misconception: reads drawing a graph as evidence about the world

questions.explanation: A graph drawn only over measured variables shows that the chosen set blocks the paths the team can see, and a path through a variable they never measured appears in no diagram at all, so the diagram cannot certify the set. Absence of a drawn arrow is a statement about what was recorded, not about what operates. What the exercise does deliver is real: it stops the team adding a collider, it identifies a mediator among the variables they did record, and it shows that a particular variable is irrelevant to the backdoor problem. Those are the errors the graph catches. The residual question, whether an unmeasured common cause remains, cannot be settled inside the diagram and has to be addressed outside it, by a design that randomises, by a mediator that carries the whole effect, or by an explicit sensitivity analysis that reports how strong an unmeasured confounder would have to be to produce what was observed.
questions.hint: A diagram over measured variables can be wrong by omission. What would an omitted variable have to look like to survive?

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a causal diagram commits a study to and what it leaves open
questions.learningObjective: explain the scope of what a causal diagram establishes
questions.stem: A team has drawn a graph of its design over the variables it measured, verified that its covariate set blocks every backdoor path in the diagram, and reported an adjusted effect. Explain what that achievement settles and what it leaves open.

answer.exemplar: What it settles is the internal coherence of the analysis. Once the graph is on the page, the team can see which of its covariates are causes of both the exposure and the outcome, which are mediators between them, and which are common effects of the two that it had been treating as ordinary controls. Each of those is a distinct error, and the last is the one that a variable list never reveals, because a collider looks exactly like a useful covariate in a regression table. Verifying that the chosen set blocks every drawn backdoor path therefore converts the analysis from a set of habits into a set of stated reasons, and a reader can disagree with a reason rather than only with a number. What it leaves open is the completeness of the diagram itself, and this is not a technicality. The graph was drawn over the variables the team measured, so a common cause of the exposure and the outcome that nobody recorded is not in the diagram, and its absence from the picture is a fact about the data collection rather than about the world. The team has shown that no drawn path survives their adjustment; it has not shown that no path survives. The three ways to address the remainder lie outside the diagram: a design that randomises and so makes every pre-exposure variable independent of assignment in expectation, a mediator structure that carries the whole effect and can be used as a front door, or a sensitivity analysis that reports how strong an unmeasured confounder would have to be to produce the estimate that was observed. The honest report states the diagram, the adjustment set, and which of those three the design has and which it lacks.

questions.explanation: A strong response separates the coherence of the analysis from the completeness of the diagram, explains that a collider among the measured covariates is the error a graph catches and a covariate list does not, and names the three remedies for unmeasured confounding with the one the design has and the ones it lacks.
questions.hint: Separate the question of whether the analysis is coherent from the question of whether the picture is complete.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Confounding strength needed to account for an observed ratio
questions.learningObjective: compute a confounder ratio and judge whether it can account for an observed ratio
questions.stem: An observational cohort reports a risk ratio of 1.60 for the exposure. A bias analysis asks what a single unmeasured common cause would have to look like: its association with the exposure is 1.25 and its association with the outcome conditional on the exposure is 1.10. Compute the risk ratio that such a confounder would produce between the exposure and the outcome. Give the answer to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: A confounder that raises the exposure rate by 1.25 and the outcome rate by 1.10 multiplies into a risk ratio of 1.25 times 1.10, which is 1.375. Whether that is enough is a comparison, not a calculation: the observed ratio is 1.60 and the confounder would account for 0.225 of the difference between no confounding at all and what was seen, so a confounder of this strength is not by itself sufficient to produce the whole of the result. Going the other way, if the association with the exposure were held at 1.25, the association with the outcome would have to reach 1.28 to account for all of it. The calculation fixes the units of the question, which is the useful part. It does not establish that the confounder exists, and it does not establish that it does not, because the answer depends on a confounder strength that nobody has measured and that a sensitivity analysis can only range over rather than pin down.
questions.hint: Multiply the two conditional associations. Then compare the product with the observed ratio.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What the propensity score is
questions.learningObjective: state what a propensity score balances
questions.stem: A study estimates the effect of a workplace training programme and has measured six candidate covariates. A colleague writes that fitting a propensity score balances the six and therefore removes confounding by all of them. What is the right response?

options.text: Balance on the score guarantees balance on the measured covariates only, so an unmeasured common cause of treatment and outcome survives a perfectly fitted model
Balance on the score guarantees balance on every possible confounder, because any confounder is a function of the covariates that predict treatment
options.misconception: claims the balance guarantee extends to unmeasured causes

options.text: Balance on the score is unnecessary, because matching on the outcome directly gives a better comparison than matching on any covariate
options.misconception: invents outcome matching as a substitute for covariate balance

options.text: The score replaces the covariates, so reporting the estimated effect without them is the preferred presentation because it is shorter
options.misconception: suggests dropping the covariates that make the score interpretable

questions.explanation: The propensity score is the probability that a unit is treated given the covariates, and the result it guarantees is narrow: units with the same score have the same distribution of every measured covariate, so balancing the score balances the whole covariate vector at once. That is why one number can stand in for six, and it is the reason the method is useful rather than the reason it is safe. The guarantee is about balance on what was measured and on nothing else, so a common cause of treatment and outcome that none of the six captures leaves the score balanced and the comparison confounded. Nor does the guarantee say the model was right, since a misspecified score can achieve balance on the covariates it was given and still be used to weight a comparison that is unbalanced in a variable it omitted.
questions.hint: Ask what is guaranteed to be equal between two units with the same score.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Propensity score from fitted logistic coefficients
questions.learningObjective: convert a fitted linear predictor into a propensity score
questions.stem: A logistic propensity model has an intercept of -0.40, a coefficient of 0.75 on a first covariate and a coefficient of -0.50 on a second. A unit has a first covariate of 1 and a second of 0. Compute that unit's fitted propensity score, to four decimal places.
questions.explanation: The linear predictor is the intercept plus each coefficient times its covariate, so here it is -0.40 plus 0.75 times 1 plus -0.50 times 0, which is 0.35. The score is that quantity put through the inverse-logistic function, one over one plus the exponential of its negative, giving 1 over 1 plus the exponential of minus 0.35, which is 0.5866. A second route writes the score as the odds divided by one plus the odds, with the odds being the exponential of 0.35, and returns the same figure. The same arithmetic reads the coefficient directly: a one-unit rise in the first covariate multiplies the odds by the exponential of 0.75, which is 2.117. A score is a model output, so its accuracy depends on which covariates went into the model and on the functional form, and the fitted distribution is worth comparing against the observed treatment rate rather than taken on trust.
questions.hint: Form the linear predictor first, then apply one over one plus the exponential of its negative.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Caliper matching and the units left unmatched
questions.learningObjective: count treated units that no unexposed unit matches within a caliper
questions.stem: Ten treated units have propensity scores of 0.11, 0.22, 0.31, 0.34, 0.52, 0.58, 0.71, 0.79, 0.88, 0.95. Ten unexposed units have scores of 0.10, 0.12, 0.30, 0.33, 0.50, 0.55, 0.70, 0.72, 0.74, 0.76. A one-to-one match is allowed only when the absolute difference between the two scores is 0.05 or less. How many treated units are left unmatched? Give the number as an integer.
questions.explanation: For each treated unit the distance to the nearest unexposed unit is 0.01, 0.08, 0.01, 0.01, 0.02, 0.03, 0.01, 0.03, 0.12, 0.19. Seven of those distances are 0.03 or less, so those seven treated units find an acceptable partner. The treated unit at 0.22 has its nearest unexposed score 0.08 away, the one at 0.88 is 0.12 away and the one at 0.95 is 0.19 away, so 3 treated units have no partner inside the caliper and 7 are matched. The caliper is doing real work rather than being a formality: the three unmatched units sit where the arms barely overlap, and dropping them narrows the population the estimate describes. Tightening the caliper to 0.01 leaves only 4 matched, and that is the trade the analyst has to make explicitly, because the unmatched units are not missing at random and the assumption behind dropping them is an assumption about that region of the score distribution rather than about the sample.
questions.hint: Take, for each treated score, the smallest distance to any unexposed score, then compare with the caliper.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Effective sample size of a weighted sample
questions.learningObjective: compute the effective sample size implied by a set of weights
questions.stem: Eight treated units have propensity scores of 0.8, 0.8, 0.4, 0.4, 0.2, 0.2, 0.6 and 0.6, and the treated share of the sample is 0.5. A stabilised weight for each unit is the treated share divided by that unit's propensity score. Compute the effective sample size of the weighted treated sample, as the square of the sum of the weights divided by the sum of their squares. Give the answer to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: The stabilised weights are 0.625, 0.625, 1.25, 1.25, 2.5, 2.5, 0.8333, 0.8333, which sum to 10.4167 and whose squares sum to 17.7951. The effective sample size is that sum squared over the sum of the squares, so it is 10.4167 squared over 17.7951, which is 6.0976. A second route returns the same figure: with the mean weight at 1.3021 the squared coefficient of variation of the weights is 0.312, and eight over one plus that is 6.0976. The number matters because a weighted sample of eight is not eight observations, it is a number of effective observations nearer 6.0976, and the standard error of a weighted mean is governed by the smaller figure, so the variance exceeds the unweighted variance by about the ratio of eight to 6.0976, that is by 1.312. The largest single weight is 2.5, and one unit carrying that much of the total is the mechanical source of the loss.
questions.hint: Square the sum of the weights and divide by the sum of the squared weights.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Standardised mean difference before weighting
questions.learningObjective: compute a standardised mean difference from group summaries
questions.stem: A covariate has a mean of 6.5 and a variance of 3.5 in the treated group and a mean of 5.1667 and a variance of 18.1667 in the unexposed group, each group holding six units. Compute the standardised mean difference before weighting, as the difference in means divided by the square root of half the sum of the two variances. Give the answer to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: The difference in means is 6.5 minus 5.1667, which is 1.3333. The pooled spread is the square root of half the sum of the two variances, that is the square root of half of 3.5 plus 18.1667, which is 3.2914. Dividing gives 0.4051. A second route computes the same quantity from the raw values in exact fractions rather than from the rounded summaries and returns the same figure. This statistic is preferred to a significance test for balance because it measures the size of the gap in units of its own spread, so a large gap in a large sample and a small gap in a small one can be compared, and it does not move with the sample size at all. A gap of a tenth of a spread is conventionally treated as negligible, and 0.4051 is well above that, so the comparison is not balanced as it stands.
questions.hint: Pool the two variances, take the square root of half their sum, and divide the mean difference by it.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Matching and weighting answer different questions
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the target of a matching analysis from the target of a weighting analysis
questions.stem: A cohort of 400 people contains 90 exposed units, and exposure cannot occur at all for people with a measured severity score above 0.7. The team must choose between matching exposed to unexposed and inverse probability weighting. What distinguishes them?

options.text: Matching leaves out exposed units that find no partner and so describes the effect among the matchable, while weighting keeps every unit but leans on large coefficients where the other arm is nearly impossible
The two are interchangeable, because both reweight the sample so that the treated and unexposed look alike on the measured covariates
options.misconception: treats two estimators of two different targets as one method

options.text: Weighting is preferable in every case, because it retains the whole sample and therefore avoids the loss of precision that discarding units causes
options.misconception: claims retaining units removes the precision cost rather than relocating it

options.text: Matching is preferable in every case, because a matched comparison is free of model dependence whereas weighting depends entirely on the fitted propensity model
options.misconception: claims one estimator is free of model dependence when both depend

questions.explanation: Matching compares each exposed unit with a small number of unexposed units that resemble it, so the units left out are those that found no partner, and how many fall is itself a measure of how far the arms fail to overlap. The resulting figure describes the effect among the exposed units that could be matched, which is a subpopulation rather than all of them. Weighting keeps every unit and pays with a coefficient, so the target is closer to an average over the whole sample, but the units in the region where one arm is nearly impossible receive large coefficients resting on a region with almost no data. Neither choice repairs the failure of positivity. They differ in which price is paid, and the choice is a decision about the target population that has to be written down rather than a technical preference settled by habit.
questions.hint: Ask which units each method discards, and whose effect the surviving units then stand for.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Average paired difference from a matched set
questions.learningObjective: compute an average treatment effect on the treated from paired differences
questions.stem: A one-to-one match produces 8 pairs, and the differences between the treated member's outcome and the matched unexposed member's outcome are 12, 7, -3, 19, 4, 25, 11, 2. Compute the average of these differences, to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: The differences sum to 77 across 8 pairs, so the average is 77 divided by 8, which is 9.62. Each pair contributes one difference rather than two observations, which is why the denominator is the number of pairs and not the number of people. The average is an effect on the treated, since the treated units define the pairs and an unmatched treated unit would contribute nothing, and it inherits the matching assumption: it is a causal quantity only if the matched unexposed unit is a credible stand-in for what that treated unit's outcome would have been. The spread of the differences tells you whether the average is worth much. Their standard deviation is 9.16 and the standard error of the average is 0.0633, giving a t statistic of 2.9707 on 7 degrees of freedom and a two-sided p of 0.0208, with a 95 per cent interval from 9.4753 to 9.7747.
questions.hint: Sum the differences and divide by the number of pairs, not by twice that number.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a caliper controls
questions.learningObjective: state what a matching caliper is for
questions.stem: A matching procedure allows a pair only when the two propensity scores differ by at most 0.02, and three treated units are dropped as a result. A reviewer asks what the 0.02 buys. What is the right answer?

options.text: It limits how far apart a matched pair may be, trading coverage of the sample for similarity within each pair, so the dropped units mark the cost
It sets the number of unexposed units available for each treated unit, so a smaller value forces one-to-one matching and a larger value allows reuse
options.misconception: confuses the caliper with the number of matches allowed

options.text: It determines the size of the matched sample, so a value below the observed spread of the scores would leave too few pairs to analyse
options.misconception: claims the caliper sets the sample size by a spread rule

options.text: It fixes the confidence interval, because a pair contributes its full distance from the caliper to the standard error of the average difference
options.misconception: invents a link between the caliper and the standard error

questions.explanation: The caliper restricts how dissimilar a pair is allowed to be, and it exists because a match far away on the score is a comparison between two kinds of unit that no design justification covers. Tightening it trades coverage for similarity: a narrower caliper leaves better-matched pairs and discards more of the sample, and the units discarded are systematically those sitting where the arms barely overlap, so the target narrows towards the region of good overlap. The three dropped units are therefore not a nuisance to be minimised but the visible cost of the assumption being made, and their number belongs in the report. A caliper of zero would be exact matching, a different procedure with different properties, so the number itself is a judgement rather than a derived quantity, and the report should say what happens to the estimate at a tighter and a looser value.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the covered population as the number gets smaller.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Two automated estimates that agree with each other and not with the strata
questions.learningObjective: compute two estimates from one cell table and their plain average
questions.stem: A cohort of 700 people is tabulated by a measured confounder Z and by exposure. At Z=0 there are 4 outcomes among 20 exposed and 8 among 80 unexposed. At Z=1 there are 100 among 500 exposed and 50 among 100 unexposed. One analysis inverse-probability-weights by a propensity model that assigns probability 0.83 at Z=0 and 0.17 at Z=1, and the other regresses the outcome on exposure alone. Compute the weighted estimate, the regression estimate, and the plain average of the two, each to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: The propensity model puts the higher probability on the stratum with the better outcome, so the weighted estimate swings well past the crude comparison: the exposed arm contributes 4 over 0.83 plus 100 over 0.17, and the unexposed arm contributes its outcome counts over the complementary probabilities, and the difference over all 700 people is 0.7097. The regression on exposure alone pools the strata and returns -0.1222, which is the crude difference of -0.1222. The plain average of the two is 0.294, which is neither. The stratum-size-weighted figure that conditions on Z throughout is -0.2429, and the three stratum differences behind it are 0.1 at Z=0 and -0.3 at Z=1. Nothing here is protected by the word doubly. Averaging two estimators is not the doubly robust construction, and the augmented form that is needs an outcome model per arm rather than two separately computed means.
questions.hint: Weight each arm's outcome counts by the reciprocal of the stated probabilities, take the difference over the whole sample, then average the two estimates.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Standardised mean difference after weighting
questions.learningObjective: compute a standardised mean difference from weighted summaries
questions.stem: Six treated units have a covariate of 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 with stabilised weights of 0.5, 0.5, 1.0, 1.0, 2.0, 2.0, and six unexposed units have values of 1, 2, 3, 4, 10, 11 with weight 1 each. The unexposed variance is 18.1667. Compute the weighted treated mean, the weighted treated variance, and the standardised mean difference using the unexposed variance, to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: The weighted treated mean is the weighted sum of the values over the sum of the weights, that is 51.5 over 7.0, giving 7.36. The weighted variance is the weighted second moment less the square of the weighted mean, and that is 56.5 less the square of 7.36, which is 2.3724. Pooling it with the unexposed variance of 18.1667 and taking the difference in means over the square root of half the sum gives 0.6835. The result is the uncomfortable one and it is the whole lesson: weighting moved the gap from 0.4051 to 0.6835, that is, in the wrong direction. Weights that rise with the treated covariate pull the weighted treated mean up, and if the model was fitted to a propensity that omitted a cause of the outcome, the correction over-corrects. Balance has to be checked after weighting rather than inferred from the fact that weighting was carried out.
questions.hint: The weighted variance is the weighted second moment minus the square of the weighted mean.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a sensitivity parameter like gamma asserts
questions.learningObjective: state what a Rosenbaum sensitivity bound commits a study to
questions.stem: A matched study reports an odds ratio of 1.90 and states that a sensitivity analysis was run at a bound of 2.0. A reader asks what that number claims. What is the right answer?

options.text: It is the factor by which the odds of treatment assignment could differ between outwardly similar units, and it bounds how far the observed odds ratio could move under that much hidden bias
It is the factor by which the true odds ratio could exceed the observed one, so a bound of 2.0 makes 1.90 as large as 17.1
options.misconception: confuses a bias multiplier with a sixteen-fold increase

options.text: It is the probability that an unmeasured confounder exists, so a bound of 2.0 means a two in three chance that the study is confounded
options.misconception: turns a sensitivity multiplier into a probability

options.text: It is the ratio of the sample size to the effective sample size after matching, so a bound of 2.0 means the analysis retained half its units
options.misconception: reuses the number for a precision quantity it does not describe

questions.explanation: The bound is a statement about the odds of treatment assignment, not about the odds of the outcome. It says assignment could be associated with treatment twice as strongly among units who look alike as chance would allow, which is the hidden bias a plausible unmeasured confounder could introduce in this design. Under that allowance the observed odds ratio could have been as large as the observed value multiplied by the bound, so a bound of 2.0 turns 1.90 into a range running from just under one up to 3.80. A range that reaches below one is the informative part of the result, because it means the sign of the conclusion is not settled by the bound, and a reader who wants to know how much hidden bias the design tolerates can read that straight off the number. The bound describes what could have happened, not what did, so it neither establishes the presence of an unmeasured confounder nor rules one out.
questions.hint: Ask whether the bound concerns how treatment was assigned or how the outcome was produced.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Extreme of a sensitivity range on an odds ratio
questions.learningObjective: compute the extreme value a sensitivity bound permits
questions.stem: A matched study observes an odds ratio of 1.90 and a sensitivity analysis is run at a bound of 2.0, meaning units who look alike could be twice as likely to be treated as chance allows. Compute the largest value the observed odds ratio could take under that bound, to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: The bound multiplies the observed odds ratio, so the largest value it permits is 1.90 times 2.0, which is 3.8. The other end of the range divides rather than multiplies, giving 1.90 over 2.0, which is 0.95, and that end is the one to look at closely. A range running from 0.95 to 3.8 contains a value of one, so under this much hidden bias the observed effect could be entirely absent, and the correct conclusion is that the design tolerates a confounder strong enough to remove the finding rather than merely to shrink it. At a milder bound of 1.5 the upper end would be 2.85, still above one, and that is the bound's practical use: it converts a worry about hidden bias into a number a reader can argue with. A bound close to 1.0 is the point at which the analysis becomes informative about the finding's robustness rather than about the confounder's absence.
questions.hint: Multiply the observed odds ratio by the bound for the upper end, and divide for the lower end.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Parallel trends as an assumption rather than a test result
questions.learningObjective: state what a pre-trend check can and cannot establish
questions.stem: Two regions are compared across a policy change: one adopted the policy and the other did not, and the pre-period trends are 0.02 and 0.01 per year. Adoption was driven by a regional officer's judgement that the two regions were diverging. A draft says the parallel-trends assumption is verified because the pre-trends are similar. What is the right response?

options.text: The check shows the pre-period series were not already diverging at the claimed rate, and the assumption itself remains untestable here because adoption was chosen for exactly that reason
The check verifies the assumption, because two pre-period trends of 0.02 and 0.01 differ by less than any effect the policy could plausibly have had
options.misconception: treats a pre-trend comparison as a verification of a counterfactual

options.text: The check refutes the assumption, because any difference at all between the two pre-period trends is a violation of parallel trends
options.misconception: demands the two pre-trends be numerically identical

options.text: The check is unnecessary, because parallel trends is guaranteed whenever the comparison group did not receive the policy during the study period
options.misconception: believes the absence of treatment guarantees parallel counterfactuals

questions.explanation: Parallel trends is an assumption about a counterfactual: absent the policy the two regions would have continued on the same path. A pre-period comparison can be consistent with that and still fail, because the failure can be a divergence that begins when the policy is announced, which is exactly the timing a pre-period check cannot see. Here the adoption criterion is itself a judgement about divergence, so the pre-trend figures come from units selected for being different and carry little reassurance. What the comparison does establish is narrower and still worth reporting: the two series were not already diverging at the rate the claimed effect is attributed to. The right response to a suspect adoption mechanism is to say so, to show results by adoption reason, and to prefer a design in which timing is set by a rule rather than by the judgement that made one group adopt first.
questions.hint: Ask when the two series would begin to diverge under the story that makes the design untrustworthy.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Two-by-two difference in differences and its standard error
questions.learningObjective: compute a difference in differences and its standard error from a cell table
questions.stem: A two-period comparison has 200 units in each cell. Before the change the comparison group had 40 events and the exposed group 60. After the change the comparison group had 50 and the exposed group 84. Compute the difference in differences on the risk scale and its standard error, each to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: The four cell risks are 0.2000 and 0.3000 before, and 0.2500 and 0.4200 after. The exposed group rose by 0.12 and the comparison group by 0.05, so the difference in differences is 0.12 minus 0.05, which is 0.07. Because the four cells are independent, the variance of the contrast is the sum of the four cell variances, each being the risk times one minus the risk divided by the cell size, giving 0.0633 after the square root. Two further routes agree: the same contrast is the interaction coefficient when the four cell means are regressed on exposure, period and their product, and a simulation of the whole design centres on 0.0701 with a spread of about 0.0642, which matches the analytic value. The z statistic is 1.106 and the two-sided p is 0.2687, so on these numbers the design does not separate the change from noise, and the 95 per cent interval runs from -0.054 to 0.194.
questions.hint: Take the change in each group, subtract one change from the other, and add the four independent cell variances.

questions.topic: An event study whose pre-period drifts
questions.learningObjective: read a dynamic effect display against the design that produced it
questions.stem: An event-study display shows the estimated effect relative to the omitted period at leads of -4, -3, -2 and -1 as 0.00, -0.02, -0.06 and -0.14, and at lags of 1, 2 and 3 as 0.18, 0.30 and 0.38. options.text: The drifting leads show the two groups were already on different paths, so the post-period movement mixes a policy effect with a divergence that predates it
The leads are all within a few hundredths of zero, so the display confirms parallel trends and the lag estimates are the policy's effect
options.misconception: reads small but moving pre-period estimates as confirmation

options.text: The leads are negative and the lags positive, so the policy reduced the outcome before adoption and raised it after, which is a consistent and interpretable pattern
options.misconception: reads a pre-period artefact as a genuine anticipation effect

options.text: The display shows the effect growing as the policy accumulated, so reporting the average over the lags understates the effect on the treated group
options.misconception: reads an unidentified trend as a dose response to the policy

questions.explanation: The leads should be zero if the two groups were on the same path before the policy, and they are not: the estimate is already at -0.14 one period before adoption and still moving. A pre-period that drifts while the post-period rises is the pattern a difference in differences produces when parallel trends fails, because the contrast is absorbing a divergence already under way. The groups were also selected asymmetrically, one because it had adopted and the other because it had not, so there is no reason to expect their untreated paths to coincide. The post-period figures cannot be read as the effect of the policy, since much of their movement is the continuation of a pre-existing trend. The display is still worth reporting, and reporting it is what makes the problem visible. The honest conclusion is that this comparison fails its own identifying assumption, and the remedy is timing set by a rule rather than by circumstance.
questions.hint: Look at the leads first. If they are not flat, the lags are not measuring the policy.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Cluster-robust inference with a handful of clusters
questions.learningObjective: compute a cluster-robust standard error and its p value on G-1 degrees of freedom
questions.stem: A study has 8 independent clusters, four assigned to treatment with mean outcomes of 0.40, 0.46, 0.38, 0.44 and four to comparison with means of 0.20, 0.24, 0.22, 0.18. Compute the difference in cluster means and divide it by the cluster-robust standard error, then give the two-sided p value referred to a t distribution on 7 degrees of freedom, to four decimal places.
questions.explanation: The treated cluster means average 0.42 and the comparison means 0.21, a difference of 0.21. The cluster-robust standard error treats the eight cluster means as the observations: square the residuals from those two group means, sum them, divide by the squared spread of the cluster labels, and apply the small-sample factor of eight over seven, which gives 0.0586. The t statistic is 3.5864 and the p value on seven degrees of freedom is 0.0089. Two comparisons put that in context. Referring the same statistic to the normal distribution would give 0.0003, roughly thirty times smaller, because the small-sample factor is the whole correction and the normal reference has no room for it. And an exact test that permutes the cluster labels, enumerating all 70 ways of choosing four of the eight as treated, gives 0.0286. The three answers bracket the truth, and the lesson is that with very few clusters the reference distribution is the decision rather than the statistic.
questions.hint: Use the cluster means as the data, then refer the t statistic to G-1 degrees of freedom rather than to the normal.

questions.topic: Already-treated units used as comparisons
questions.learningObjective: explain why a staggered adoption can bias a two-group comparison
questions.stem: A policy is adopted in three regions in successive years, and the study compares every adopting region with the single region that never adopts, pooling all years. A colleague notes that a region that adopted early is used as a comparison for one that adopts later. What is the concern?

options.text: An early adopter is already treated when a later one adopts, so using it as a comparison lets the policy's own effect enter the contrast and narrows or reverses the estimate
The concern runs the other way, because a unit that has already adopted is a purer comparison for a later adopter than a never-adopter is
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the contamination

options.text: There is no concern, because the comparison region never adopted and so its untreated status is guaranteed for every period of the study
options.misconception: forgets that the treated regions are also used as comparisons

options.text: The concern is the sample size, because pooling three treated regions against one comparison leaves the comparison with too few units for a stable standard error
options.misconception: recasts a bias problem as a precision problem

questions.explanation: Once an early adopter has taken the policy it is no longer untreated, so using it against a later adopter puts a treated unit into the comparison group and lets part of the policy's own effect on the outcome appear in the contrast. The contamination narrows the gap and in the limit can reverse its sign. Pooling across years with a single never-adopting comparison is the version of the design most exposed to it. Restricting each comparison to units still untreated at that moment removes the contamination and is what a modern estimator does, at the cost of weighting the later adopters less. Staggered adoption does not ruin the design, but the estimator has to be chosen with the timing pattern in mind and the choice stated in the paper.
questions.hint: Ask, for each treated unit, what the comparison group consists of at that unit's own adoption date.

questions.topic: Level shift and slope change in a segmented series
questions.learningObjective: estimate a level shift and a slope change from a segmented series
questions.stem: A monthly series of 24 observations averages 20.05 over the twelve months before an intervention and 26.77 over the twelve after it, with a clear change in trend at the intervention. Fit a segmented regression with an intercept, a linear time trend, a step indicator for the twelve months after the intervention, and the product of that indicator with time. Compute the coefficient on the step indicator, the coefficient on the time trend, and the coefficient on the step-by-time product, each to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: Centring time on the intervention so the cut sits at zero, the four coefficients come out at 2.8709 for the step, 0.0133 for the underlying trend and 0.5671 for the change in trend per month. The step is a level shift and the product term is the change in slope, and they answer different questions: the first says the series jumped, the second says it then climbed faster. They are estimated jointly rather than from the two period means, and the period means differ by 6.72, which is larger than the step of 2.8709 because most of that gap is the accumulation of the faster climb rather than an initial jump. The step's standard error is 0.376 and its t statistic 7.6359, so the jump is estimated precisely. Precision is not identification: a segmented series with one treated unit and no comparison cannot rule out that something else changed at the same moment, and a control series is what would.
questions.hint: Fit the four terms together; the step and the change in trend are separate coefficients.

questions.topic: What a single interrupted series cannot separate

questions.stem: A drug's prescribing rate is charted monthly for four years. A guideline is issued in month 31 and the series shows a rise afterwards. A draft concludes the guideline caused the rise. What is the defect?

options.text: Nothing in the design separates the guideline from any other change at that date, so the series documents what happened without showing what caused it
The defect is the monthly interval, because a guideline cannot plausibly change behaviour within a month of being issued
options.misconception: objects to the measurement interval rather than the lack of a comparison

options.text: The defect is the length of the series, because four years of post-issue data would be needed before the trend could be attributed to the guideline
options.misconception: prescribes a longer follow-up as though that supplied a comparison

options.text: There is no defect, because a change in level at exactly the intervention date is itself the identification the design requires
options.misconception: treats the timing of the change as sufficient attribution

questions.explanation: The series has one treated unit and no comparison, so the guideline is not separated from anything else that changed in month 31: a new drug, a coding change, a media story, a reimbursement change or a trend already bending upward would all produce the same picture. Segmenting the series estimates a level shift and a change in slope in the observed line and nothing more, because with one series the model cannot attribute either to the intervention. The design becomes informative when a comparison series unaffected by the guideline is charted over the same months and the two are differenced, which is why applied interrupted series studies are nearly always comparative. Reporting the segmented coefficients without a comparison still documents the timing and size of what changed, and the honest claim is that something changed at the intervention, not that the intervention changed it.

questions.topic: Discontinuity at a threshold from a local linear fit
questions.learningObjective: estimate a discontinuity by extrapolating a local linear fit to the threshold
questions.stem: An eligibility score is cut at 100. Below the cut, five units score 99.1, 99.3, 99.5, 99.7, 99.9 with outcomes 9.4, 10.0, 10.6, 11.2, 11.8. Above the cut, five units score 100.1, 100.3, 100.5, 100.7, 100.9 with outcomes 14.4, 15.0, 15.6, 16.2, 16.8. Fit a straight line to each side and evaluate it at the cut. Compute the estimated discontinuity, to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: The line through the five points below the cut has a slope of 3.0 and, extrapolated to a score of 100, a fitted value of 12.1. The line through the five points above has a slope of 3.0 and a fitted value of 14.1 at the same point. The estimated discontinuity is the difference, 14.1 minus 12.1, which is 2.0. Two checks agree. A single regression of all ten points on a step indicator and a separate score slope on each side returns the same 2.0 for the step, and narrowing the window to the three points nearest the cut on each side also returns 2.0, because both sides are exactly linear over this range so the fit does not depend on where the window ends. That insensitivity to the bandwidth is the behaviour a well-behaved design should show, and it is worth reporting at more than one bandwidth precisely because designs driven by a handful of points do not have it. The identifying assumption is continuity of the outcome in the score at the cut, and the estimate compares just above with just below rather than with anyone treated.
questions.hint: Fit a line on each side, evaluate both at the threshold, and take the difference.
