questions.topic: What a regression discontinuity design buys
questions.learningObjective: state the identifying assumption behind a regression discontinuity estimate
questions.stem: A benefits eligibility is cut at a score of 100, and a study estimates the effect of eligibility by comparing outcomes just below with outcomes just above the cut. A reviewer asks what could still go wrong. What is the right answer?

options.text: The design rests on units either side of the cut being alike apart from eligibility, and sorting, anticipation or an outcome that jumps for its own reasons would each break that
The design is invalid unless the score has no gaps near the cut, because a gap would mean the two sides are not adjacent in the data
options.misconception: treats a sparse score distribution as disqualifying

options.text: The design is valid only if the cut was set before the outcome data were collected, because a cut chosen afterwards can be moved to suit the result
options.misconception: makes the timing of the rule setting the identifying assumption

options.text: The design is valid only for outcomes measured continuously, because a binary outcome cannot produce a discontinuity estimate
options.misconception: claims the outcome scale restricts the design

questions.explanation: The design converts a causal question into a comparison of two groups defined by a rule rather than by a choice, and the whole estimate rests on the claim that units just above the cut and units just below it are alike apart from the treatment. That claim is a continuity assumption, and it is not testable in the data because the two sides have no overlap in the score. Three things can break it without anyone breaking the rule: the outcome could have a discontinuity at the threshold for reasons of their own, units just below the cut could respond to anticipating it, and units could sort themselves around it. Each leaves the same signature as a treatment effect. The design is not weak for being untestable, since the alternative designs are weaker for a different reason, but it is weak in this specific way and the report should say which threats were checked and which were not.
questions.hint: Ask what would have to be true of the score distribution for the comparison to mean anything.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Fuzzy discontinuity at a threshold
questions.learningObjective: compute a fuzzy discontinuity estimate from a threshold design
questions.stem: An eligibility score is cut at a value that divides 200 units below from 200 above. Below the cut 120 units are eligible and 145 have the outcome; above the cut 180 units are eligible and 175 have the outcome. The share eligible is 0.6 below and 0.9 above, and the outcome rate is 0.725 below and 0.875 above. Compute the jump in the outcome rate, the jump in the eligibility rate, and the ratio of the first to the second, each to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: The outcome rate rises from 0.725 to 0.875, a jump of 0.15, while the eligible share rises from 0.6 to 0.9, a jump of 0.3. The ratio is 0.15 over 0.3, which is 0.5. That ratio is the fuzzy discontinuity estimate, and it is the effect for the units whose eligibility actually changed at the cut, since those are the only units the comparison can speak about. A second route returns the same number: treating the side of the cut as an instrument for eligibility and running two-stage least squares of the outcome on eligibility gives 0.5 as well. The construction is internally consistent, since the jump in the outcome should equal the jump in eligibility multiplied by the effect on those who switch, and 0.3 times 0.5 is 0.15. What the estimate cannot say is anything about units far from the cut, since only 0.3 of the units change eligibility there.
questions.hint: Divide the jump in the outcome by the jump in eligibility, not the other way round.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Which instrumental variable assumption cannot be tested
questions.learningObjective: identify the instrumental variable assumption that data cannot check
questions.stem: A study uses a randomisation of lottery ticket allocation as an instrument for whether a unit received a place on a training programme. The first stage is strong, with an F statistic well above any conventional threshold, and the balance of background characteristics across the instrument is good. What is still assumed rather than established?

options.text: That the instrument affects the outcome only through treatment, which no balance check or first-stage statistic can establish because holding treatment fixed is exactly what the data cannot do
That the instrument is unrelated to background characteristics, which the balance check addresses directly and which the design therefore establishes
options.misconception: names a checked assumption as the untestable one

options.text: That the instrument is strong enough to identify the effect, which the first stage F statistic establishes whenever it is above ten
options.misconception: names a checked assumption as the untestable one

options.text: That the units assigned by the instrument comply with it, which cannot be checked because adherence is only visible for those who were assigned
options.misconception: mistakes a compliance rate for the exclusion restriction

questions.explanation: Three assumptions carry an instrumental variable estimate. That the instrument shifts treatment, the first stage, is the one the F statistic addresses. That the instrument is balanced on background characteristics and so is unrelated to anything that also moves the outcome, the independence, is what the balance check addresses. The third is that the instrument moves the outcome only by changing treatment, and no amount of data speaks to it, because the only way to observe the instrument's effect on the outcome while holding treatment fixed is to find units that did not take the treatment the instrument assigned, and comparing those to the rest tells you about them rather than about the instrument. The failure has a name, the exclusion restriction, and it cannot be tested in the data at hand. A design in which the instrument could act on the outcome directly, such as a lottery that also confers a benefit, does not admit this instrument at all.
questions.hint: Ask what the balance check on background characteristics can and cannot rule out.

questions.topic: First-stage strength and a two-stage estimate
questions.learningObjective: compute a first-stage F statistic and a two-stage least squares estimate
questions.stem: An instrument takes the value 0 for 100 units and 1 for 100 units. Treatment is received by 70 of the second hundred and 30 of the first. The mean outcome is 4.1 where the instrument is 0 and 5.3 where it is 1. Regress treatment on the instrument, then use the fitted treatment values to predict the outcome. Compute the first-stage F statistic and the resulting two-stage least squares estimate, each to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: Regressing treatment on the instrument gives a slope of 0.4 and an intercept of 0.3, so the mean treatment rate is 0.3 where the instrument is 0 and 0.7 where it is 1. The standard error of that slope is 0.06513, giving a t of 6.1412 and an F of 37.714, which is the first-stage strength. Dividing the outcome's covariance with the instrument by the treatment's covariance with it gives the two-stage estimate, and that is 3.0. Two routes agree: solving the instrument moment condition directly returns 3.0, and the complier effect built into this table is also 3. Ordinary least squares on the same data returns -0.6, the wrong sign entirely, because treated and untreated units differ in ways the instrument does not. That contrast is the entire argument for the design.
questions.hint: Divide the covariance of the outcome with the instrument by the covariance of treatment with the instrument.

questions.topic: An instrument that changes the outcome by another route
questions.learningObjective: recognise a violation of the exclusion restriction
questions.stem: A study uses eligibility for a free smoking-cessation course, allocated when a clinic ran out of places, as an instrument for actually taking the course. The first stage is strong and eligibility is unrelated to smoking, income and age. The course is offered at a time when participants take a paid leave day. The estimated effect of taking the course on relapse is 22 percentage points, against an observational estimate of 9. What is the defect?

options.text: Eligibility also delivers a paid day that could itself change relapse, so the estimate mixes the course with the day off and no amount of first-stage strength or balance addresses it
The defect is the weak first stage, since an F statistic well above ten does not guarantee identification when the outcome is a proportion
options.misconception: invents a first-stage objection the design does not have

options.text: The defect is the observational comparison, which should have been discarded because an estimate near 9 is too small to be credible
options.misconception: discards a figure for being small rather than for a stated reason

options.text: There is no defect, because a paid day off is part of receiving the course and therefore falls inside the treatment the instrument is standing in for
options.misconception: redefines the treatment after the fact to preserve the estimate

questions.explanation: The course is not the only thing eligibility delivers, because being offered a place also entitles a participant to the paid day, and the paid day is exactly the kind of thing that could change whether someone relapses. The estimate therefore mixes the effect of the course with the effect of the day off, and it moves the estimate away from the effect of taking the course, which is why it is the larger of the two figures rather than the smaller. The strong first stage and the balance of eligibility on background characteristics are both satisfied and neither helps, because the problem lies in a mechanism the balance check cannot see. questions.topic: Intention to treat against per protocol
questions.learningObjective: recover a per-protocol effect from an intention-to-treat contrast and a compliance rate
questions.stem: A programme is assigned to 100 units and 80 of them take it up, with an outcome rate of 0.30 among the 80 and 0.50 among the 20 who do not. Another 100 units are assigned to nothing and all of them have an outcome rate of 0.50. Compute the intention-to-treat effect and the per-protocol effect among those who took the programme up, each to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: The assigned group averages -0.16, since 80 units at 0.30 and 20 at 0.50 give a pooled rate of 0.34 against 0.50 in the comparison, a difference of -0.16. That is the intention-to-treat effect, and it is what a randomised comparison delivers. The units that took the programme up differ from the comparison group in at least one respect, namely that they took it up, and the gap between 0.30 and 0.50 is the per-protocol effect, which is -0.2. Recovering it from the assigned comparison requires dividing by the compliance difference of 0.80, and -0.16 over 0.80 is -0.2, the same figure. That agreement is the check on the arithmetic, and it holds only because every unit took the treatment in proportion to the assignment. Where some assigned to the programme take it anyway, the two estimates separate and neither can be read off the other.
questions.hint: Divide the intention-to-treat effect by the share that took the programme up.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a mediation analysis has to assume
questions.learningObjective: state the assumptions behind a product-of-coefficients mediation estimate
questions.stem: A study fits the mediator on the exposure, then the outcome on the exposure and the mediator, and reports the product of the two coefficients as the indirect effect. A reviewer asks what that product is assuming. What is the right answer?

options.text: It requires no unmeasured common cause of the exposure and the mediator, none of the mediator and the outcome given the exposure, and no mediator-outcome confounder that the exposure itself affects
It requires only that the mediator be measured without error, since the two coefficients already contain the effect of every unmeasured variable
options.misconception: reduces a causal identification problem to measurement alone

options.text: It requires that the sample be large enough for the product to be precise, since the interpretation follows from the confidence interval rather than the point estimate
options.misconception: makes a sample-size condition carry an interpretation

options.text: It requires nothing beyond correct model specification, because a linear model of the outcome on the exposure and the mediator identifies the indirect effect by construction
options.misconception: claims linear identification is automatic

questions.explanation: The product is the indirect effect only under assumptions that are strong and largely about the unobserved. It requires that the exposure cause the mediator, that the mediator cause the outcome once the exposure is held fixed, that there be no unmeasured common cause of the exposure and the mediator, and no unmeasured common cause of the mediator and the outcome once the exposure is held fixed. The last two are the sequential ignorability conditions and they cannot be checked, because the variables involved are by definition unmeasured. There is a further structural condition: a mediator-outcome confounder that is itself caused by the exposure opens a path the product does not represent, and in that case the product is not a natural indirect effect at all. The analysis is still worth running, and reporting the two paths separately is more informative than reporting the product, but the product carries an interpretation that has to be stated rather than assumed by the reader.

questions.topic: Indirect effect from the product of two coefficients
questions.learningObjective: compute an indirect effect and its interval from two fitted coefficients
questions.stem: A fitted model of the mediator on the exposure gives a coefficient of 0.45 with a standard error of 0.03. A fitted model of the outcome on the exposure and the mediator gives 0.7 for the mediator with a standard error of 0.05, and 0.285 for the exposure. A model of the outcome on the exposure alone gives a total effect of 0.600. Compute the indirect effect and the proportion of the total effect it accounts for, each to three decimal places.

The direct effect is 0.285 and the total is 0.600, and the two paths sum: 0.285 plus 0.315 is 0.6, which is the total from the model with the exposure alone. That identity is the check on the arithmetic, and it holds in a linear model with no interaction between the exposure and the mediator. The proportion mediated is 0.525. A standard error for the product comes from the delta method, treating the two coefficients as independent, which is 0.0308, giving a 95 per cent interval from 0.255 to 0.375. The two assumptions behind that calculation are visible in it: independence of the two coefficient estimates, and a linear model with no exposure-mediator interaction.

The direct effect checks the division: 0.285 over 0.600 is 0.475, and the two shares sum to one, which is the arithmetic that confirms the denominator was the right one. The total has to come from a model that excludes the mediator, because including the mediator replaces the total with the direct effect and makes the proportion come out as one. What the proportion means is that slightly over half of the effect in this model runs through the mediator and the remainder does not, under the same set of assumptions the indirect effect needed. A proportion near one half is not a statement that the pathway is important in policy terms, since the size of the total effect is a separate matter and a large share of a trivial effect is still trivial.

options.text: The product is unaffected provided the mediator is measured at a single time point, since repeated measurement is what would introduce the shared cause
options.misconception: invents a measurement-frequency source for the confounding

What results is not a decomposition of the total effect into a part that runs through the mediator and a part that does not, because the total effect on the outcome now includes the mediated part and the shared-cause part and they are not separable. Reporting the two path coefficients separately is still informative and is what the paper should do; the product is the quantity that needs the assumption, and the assumption is the one that has just been shown to be doubtful.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: The components of an emulated target trial
questions.learningObjective: list what a target trial emulation has to specify
questions.stem: A registry cohort is analysed as though it were a trial that had been run, comparing units assigned a guideline with units not assigned it. Put these specifications in the order a target trial emulation sets them out.

options.text: The eligibility criteria, and the time origin from which follow-up is counted for every unit in the same way
The assignment strategy, and whether it was randomised or determined by something the investigators observed
The strategies for follow-up start time, for assignment, and for the handling of events that occur before the assigned strategy is implemented
The outcome measures and the time horizon, fixed before the contrast is computed so that the choice cannot follow the result
The analysis plan, naming whether the estimand is the intention-to-treat or the per-protocol contrast and how adherence will be handled

questions.explanation: The order is the order of a protocol, because an emulation has to commit to the same decisions a real trial would have committed to before anyone looked, and the reason for doing it on registry data is precisely that the decisions are recoverable. Eligibility criteria come first because they fix who the trial would have enrolled, and everything after is conditional on that. Assignment strategy comes next, because whether the strategy was randomised, or allocated in some other way, determines what the comparison can support. The strategies for follow-up start time, assignment, and the handling of events that happen before the assigned strategy is implemented are the ones most often left implicit, and leaving them implicit is what allows units who never took the assigned strategy to be counted as though they had. Outcome measures and the analysis plan come last and are the easiest, and the analysis plan is where the intention-to-treat and per-protocol estimands are declared. A real trial writes all of this in a protocol; an emulation that writes it after the fact has still fixed it, just later and without the protection.
questions.hint: Ask which of these decisions a real trial protocol fixes before recruitment opens.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Intention-to-treat analogue in an emulated target trial
questions.learningObjective: compute an intention-to-treat analogue by assignment
questions.stem: An emulated target trial starts from 1000 eligible units. 600 are assigned a guideline and 500 of them actually receive it; 100 of the 400 not assigned receive it anyway. Among units who receive the guideline the outcome rate is 0.20 and among those who do not it is 0.35. Compute the intention-to-treat analogue of the effect, comparing by assignment rather than by receipt, to four decimal places.
questions.explanation: The assigned group has an outcome rate of 0.225, since 500 units at 0.20 and 100 at 0.35 give 135 events across 600 units. The not-assigned group has a rate of 0.3125, since 100 at 0.20 and 300 at 0.35 give 125 events across 400 units. The difference is -0.0875. That is the intention-to-treat analogue and it is the default estimand of an emulated trial, because assignment rather than receipt is what the design controls. For comparison, the per-protocol analogue comparing by receipt is -0.15, a larger effect, because the units who receive the guideline differ from those who do not in ways that receipt does not control. The compliance difference is 0.5833, and dividing the intention-to-treat analogue by it gives -0.15, which recovers the per-protocol figure, so the two are consistent with each other even though they answer different questions. The two arms sum to 1000 units and the events to 260, which is the check that the table adds up.
questions.hint: Average within the assigned arms, using every unit in the arm, not only those who received the guideline.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What an E-value is a statement about
questions.learningObjective: state what an E-value commits a reader to comparing
questions.stem: An observational cohort reports a risk ratio of 1.60 with a 95 per cent interval running from 1.20 to 2.40, and states that the E-value for the interval limit nearest the null is 1.69. What does that number mean?

options.text: It is the association an unmeasured confounder would need with the exposure and with the outcome, in the same direction, for the observed ratio to be explained away
It is the probability that the study is confounded, so a value of 1.69 means a sixty-nine per cent chance the result is spurious
options.misconception: reads a sensitivity multiplier as a probability

options.text: It is the number of unmeasured confounders compatible with the data, so a value of 1.69 means two confounder sets fit the observed result
options.misconception: turns a strength into a count of confounder sets

options.text: It is the ratio of the sample size to the effective sample size after weighting, so a value of 1.69 means the analysis retained fifty-nine per cent of its units
options.misconception: reuses the number for a precision quantity

questions.explanation: The E-value is the strength of association that an unmeasured confounder would need with both the exposure and the outcome, above and beyond the measured covariates, for the observed risk ratio to be explained away. It is a translation of a result into the units of the threat the study cannot rule out, which is why it is reported alongside the interval rather than instead of it. A larger E-value means the estimate is harder to dismiss on those grounds, and the number to look at is the one for the interval limit nearest the null, because that is the limit that would have to move to reach a ratio of one. Its limitation is specific and worth stating: it assumes the confounder is associated with the exposure and the outcome in the same direction and not with the measurement of either, so it understates the required confounding when the threat runs the other way or through error in a measured covariate.
questions.hint: Ask what would have to be true of an unmeasured confounder for the observed ratio to be nothing but confounding.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: E-value for the interval limit nearest the null
questions.learningObjective: compute an E-value from a risk ratio and its confidence limit
questions.stem: A risk ratio of 1.60 arrives with a 95 per cent interval from 1.20 to 2.40. For a ratio above one the E-value is the ratio plus the square root of the ratio times the ratio less one. Compute the E-value for the confidence limit nearer the null, to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: The limit nearer the null is the lower one, 1.20, since it is the closer of the two to a ratio of one. The E-value is 1.20 plus the square root of 1.20 times 0.20, which is 1.20 plus the square root of 0.24, and that is 1.6899. A second route inverts the same relationship: searching for the ratio whose E-value is 1.6899 returns 1.20, and the same inversion of the point estimate's E-value of 2.5798 returns 1.60. The number to read is this one rather than the point estimate's, because the lower limit is the one that would have to move to reach a ratio of one. Two things the figure does not do are worth recording. It does not say the unmeasured confounder exists, since it describes what would have to be true rather than what is, and it assumes the confounder acts in the same direction on both the exposure and the outcome and is not entangled with a measured covariate, so a threat of either kind needs a different calculation.
questions.hint: Take the confidence limit closer to one, then add the square root of the ratio times the ratio less one.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Confounding strength that would account for an observed ratio
questions.learningObjective: solve for the confounder strength that would explain an observed ratio
questions.stem: A cohort reports a risk ratio of 1.60 for the exposure, and a bias analysis assumes one unmeasured confounder associated with the exposure at a risk ratio of 1.30. Compute the association the confounder would need with the outcome, conditional on the exposure, for it to account for the whole of the observed ratio, to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: The confounder's contributions multiply, so an exposure association of 1.30 combined with an outcome association of u produces 1.30 times u. Setting that equal to the observed 1.60 gives u of 1.60 divided by 1.30, which is 1.2308. Multiplying back confirms it: 1.30 times 1.2308 is 1.6, the observed ratio. The exercise converts an unanswerable question into a range, because the analyst can now say that a confounder of this strength would be needed, and a reader who thinks that unlikely has said something specific. Two cautions keep it from being a licence to dismiss the result. The calculation assumes a single confounder with no measurement error in the measured covariates, and both assumptions make the required strength too small, because real studies usually face several partly overlapping confounder paths and covariates measured with error. It also fixes the direction: a confounder working the other way would have to be stronger still, not weaker, to produce the same ratio.
questions.hint: Divide the observed ratio by the association the confounder is assumed to have with the exposure.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a negative control is for
questions.learningObjective: state the function of a negative control outcome or exposure
questions.stem: A study of a new clinical handover procedure includes a negative control outcome that the procedure could not plausibly affect, and a negative control exposure assigned by a route unrelated to the exposure of interest. What are these for?

options.text: They turn an untestable worry about confounding or bias into a testable prediction, and a failure on the control points to a problem the main analysis cannot see
They increase the precision of the main estimate by adding observations that are known to carry no signal
options.misconception: mistakes a bias check for a precision device

options.text: They confirm the analysis pipeline is correct, because a procedure that reproduces the negative control has been shown to be unbiased
options.misconception: claims one correct negative control establishes the absence of bias

options.text: They are required for publication, since a study without them cannot demonstrate that its positive finding is not a multiple-comparison artefact
options.misconception: invents a publication requirement

questions.explanation: A negative control is a comparison the hypothesis predicts nothing about, and a departure from that prediction is informative in a way an ordinary check is not. If the handover procedure cannot affect the negative control outcome and it does, then something other than the procedure is producing the association: residual confounding, selection, measurement or a coding error. The same logic runs through a negative control exposure, which should predict nothing but does, and locating the problem is then a matter of which variables it shares with the failed control. The value is that a negative control converts an untestable worry into a testable one, in the same spirit as a placebo arm or a manipulation check. Its limitation is that it detects bias without diagnosing it, and it is silent about the cases where the bias happens to spare the control.
questions.hint: Ask what the study predicts about a variable it claims cannot be involved.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Selection into a study measured against a whole cohort
questions.learningObjective: compute how selection changes a risk ratio
questions.stem: A cohort of 1000 people contains 200 exposed and 800 unexposed, with 100 cases among the exposed and 100 among the unexposed. A study is then conducted on a 400-person subsample whose selection depends on both exposure and case status: it contains 50 exposed cases, 50 exposed non-cases, 25 unexposed cases and 275 unexposed non-cases. Compute the risk ratio in the whole cohort and the risk ratio in the selected sample, each to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: In the whole cohort the risk among the exposed is 100 over 200, that is 0.5, and among the unexposed 100 over 800, that is 0.125, so the risk ratio is 4.0. In the sample the exposed total is 50 plus 50, that is 100, and the unexposed total is 25 plus 275, that is 300, giving a sample risk ratio of 50 over 100 against 25 over 300, which is 6.0. The ratio between them is 1.5, so selection has moved the estimate away from the cohort value by a factor of one and a half without changing a single outcome. The mechanism is visible in the selection probabilities: the sample keeps half the exposed units whether or not they are cases, but only 0.25 of the unexposed cases against 0.39 of the unexposed non-cases, so it disproportionately discards unexposed non-cases and thereby raises the unexposed risk. Selection that depends on the outcome is the dangerous kind, and correcting for it requires information about the selection that the sample does not contain.
questions.hint: Compute each risk ratio from its own denominators, then take the ratio of the two.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Effect modification distinguished from confounding
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a modifier of treatment effect from a confounder of it
questions.stem: A study finds that a treatment's effect differs between two age groups, and the age difference is the same in a randomised trial and in an observational cohort. A second variable differs between the arms only in the cohort, and adjusting for it does not change the age interaction. What follows?

options.text: Age modifies the effect and the second variable confounds it, since the first difference survives randomisation and the second does not, and adjusting for a confounder does not remove a modifier
Both are confounders, since any variable associated with treatment and with the outcome must be adjusted for regardless of how the association arose
options.misconception: ignores what randomisation tells about the source of an association

options.text: Both are modifiers, since a difference in effect between subgroups is by definition a modification of the effect of the treatment
options.misconception: declares a confounder a modifier on the strength of a subgroup difference

options.text: Neither needs to be reported, since adjustment removes confounding and the age interaction is already visible in the stratified figures
options.misconception: dismisses a subgroup finding rather than interpreting it

questions.explanation: The two variables play different structural roles and the ways the results behave separate them. The age difference reproduces itself under randomisation, so it is a property of how the treatment works rather than an artefact of how the groups were formed, and adjusting for a modifier is not what identifies a causal effect. The second difference disappears under randomisation, so it is a difference in who ended up in which arm, and adjusting for it removes a spurious association. That the age interaction is unchanged by the adjustment is the informative observation: it says the two are not competing explanations of the same number. The consequence for generalisation is separate again. A modifier limits the transport of an effect from the trial's population to another, since the average effect in one age group need not hold in another, whereas a confounder has to be removed before any effect is estimated at all.
questions.hint: Ask whether the difference would have been there if treatment had been assigned by chance.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: An observational claim that outruns its design
questions.learningObjective: appraise a causal claim against the design that produced it
questions.stem: A cohort of 40,000 records over six years reports that people who take up a leisure activity have 18 per cent lower cardiovascular risk than those who do not, adjusted for age, sex, income, smoking, body mass index and prior diagnosis, with a hazard ratio of 0.82 and a 95 per cent interval of 0.79 to 0.85. The conclusion reads: taking up the activity reduces cardiovascular risk. What is the defect?

options.text: The exposure was chosen rather than assigned and the adjustment list is a statement about handled differences, so an 0.82 hazard ratio supports an association rather than the causal claim the sentence makes
The interval is too narrow, because a hazard ratio below one that many observations apart from one should be reported with a wider interval to allow for selection
options.misconception: objects to precision as though a wide interval would be more accurate

options.text: The cohort is too short, because six years of follow-up cannot detect cardiovascular effects that take longer to appear
options.misconception: raises a follow-up objection without addressing the confounding

options.text: The adjustment set is too small, because a list of six covariates cannot capture the confounding in a cohort of this size and more covariates would fix it
options.misconception: treats the number of covariates as the remedy for an unmeasured cause

questions.explanation: Three features of the design set the ceiling on the claim. The exposure was not assigned, so the comparison is between people who chose to take the activity and people who did not, and a covariate list is a statement about which differences were handled rather than proof that none remain. Physical capacity is the obvious candidate: people who can take up an activity at all differ systematically from those who cannot, and that variable is a cause of both the uptake and the outcome, so the measured adjustment set leaves the pathway open. Relatedly, the covariates are measured once, and a diagnosis made before the activity was taken up can be a consequence of an intention to take it. And the interval is narrow because 40,000 records make a biased estimate precise, which is the specific trap of a large observational dataset. The defensible claim is an association of 0.82 among people who could plausibly have taken the activity up, with the covariate list stated and the unmeasured-confounding risk named.
questions.hint: Ask which cause of both the activity and the outcome is absent from the adjustment list.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Writing a causal claim that matches the design
questions.learningObjective: explain how to state a causal claim at the strength the design supports
questions.stem: A cohort study with a large sample, a narrow interval and a list of six adjusted covariates reports an association of 0.82 and concludes that the exposure reduces the outcome. Explain how the same result should be worded, and what each part of the wording commits the authors to.

answer.exemplar: The problem is not the estimate, which may well be reported accurately, and not the interval, which is computed correctly for the model that was fitted. The problem is the verb. An observational design licenses a statement about what happened to the units who were studied, and a causal statement about what would happen if the exposure were changed is licensed only by a design that supports it. Three commitments are at stake and each needs its own sentence. The first is the design: the exposure was chosen by the units rather than assigned, so any comparison is between people who differ before the exposure in ways the analysis may not have handled, and the wording should say the exposure was not assigned. The second is the adjustment set: naming the six covariates states which differences were accounted for and implies nothing about the rest, so the wording should give the list and should not imply that adjustment settled the question. The third is the precision: a narrow interval with 40,000 records makes a biased estimate precise, and precision about a quantity that is not the causal one is not evidence about the causal one. So a defensible statement runs: among adults who could have taken up the exposure, those who did had a cardiovascular event rate 18 per cent lower over six years, adjusted for age, sex, income, smoking, body mass index and prior diagnosis, and unmeasured confounding by physical capacity cannot be ruled out. That sentence is weaker than the original, and it is also the strongest claim the design carries. Anything stronger, including a hedged version that says the authors believe causation while noting limitations, misleads a reader who reads the first clause.

questions.explanation: A strong response names the exposure as chosen rather than assigned, gives the covariate list as the set of handled differences, and separates precision about the association from any claim about a causal effect.
questions.hint: Replace the causal verb with the design's own terms, then add what was adjusted for and what was not.
